I worked the night-shift, and then we went back to our village, and we were -- together with my friend, and we were arrested and taken to the village of Pozhare. This is what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Radosevic. If you can confine yourself to answering my questions, we will move along more swiftly. Now, the question I asked you was to confirm that what is recorded in that statement is not true. It's not the truth, is it? The first three lines of that statement in which it records that you said you'd fled Dashinoc with your mother after the KLA turned up in your village, that's not right, is it? That didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say it to her or did she make that up?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To whom? To the NGO?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Did you -- this was a document written by a woman who has a number in this case, 28, and I'm asking you whether you said that to her at the time or whether she made that up?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I gave the statement to the effect that on the 21st of April, I was in the village of Dasinovac, that I went home, and that in the morning I went with my mother and that we were arrested by the terrorist soldiers in Pozare. So let me say once again: They can write whatever they want, but let me say once again: On the 21st of April, I was in the village of Dasinovac. I took my mother to see her doctor, so I did not see Novak at all on that day. The next day, I met Novak and he said that he would come with us by car, in our car, and in Pozare we were captured. She may have changed the story. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. It's not possible that you told her that, then?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother may have said, or maybe Novak said something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is an interview with you and you alone, Mr. Radosevic. Is it possible that you told her that you'd run away from the village in fear of the KLA, or is it not possible that you told her that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told her that I fled from the village on the 22nd, after I'd surrendered the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did you tell her you fled to the youth camp in Decan, or did she make that up?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She did not make that up. I told her that I had accommodation in the youth camp, that I just spent the night there, and that in the morning I went to the village of Dasinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me ask you a little bit about the background to the people that you saw out on the road in Pozhare and along the way. I just want to ask you some questions about the background. Mr. Dutertre has taken you to a passage in the report published by that NGO which deals with your position and the death of your father. You've seen that passage, haven't you? The single sheet you have. Yes?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you will have seen from the screen that that is a passage from a much longer report. I just want to ask you this: Had you yourself heard about what had taken place in Drenica, in Likoshan and Prekaz at the end of February, beginning of March?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard from the news reports; I read it in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did you read that 80 Kosovar Albanians, including women and children, had been killed?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I had not heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you hear that at Qirez and Likoshan, 12 people were arrested, taken out, and put to death by the Serb forces? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did you know that at Prekaz, amongst 37 people killed were 11 children and seven women? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. And all of this had happened just a few weeks before the incident you're describing, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did hear about that, but I didn't believe in that. I can only tell you what happened when I was captured and what happened to my family. Now, as to what happened in those other areas, I cannot tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Radosevic, I'm asking you about the attitude and behaviour of the Albanian villagers that you saw out on the street and what it was that was behind the way that you have described them behaving. So can I ask you about the 24th of March and the police action in Gllogjan on the 24th of March. You've mentioned that in your evidence already. Were you aware of what took place in Gllogjan on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard the next day that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That a police officer called Otovic had been killed; yes?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you hear that three Albanian teenagers had been shot running away from the village?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer that question. I'm not the person who can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You know, don't you, some of the police officers who were involved in that operation, personally; you knew them at the time?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know all of them by sight. I can't not know them. But I'm not sure they participated in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Some of your friends participated in it, didn't they, Mr. Radosevic?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which friends?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Momo Stijovic, for example. He's a friend of yours, isn't he? Or he was?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you got that from.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is he related to Novak Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two persons called Momo Stijovic. Maybe you got some wrong information.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Novak Stijovic has a brother called Momo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was he a police officer?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were there other police officers in the Stijovic family?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Do you know who Zoran Stijovic is?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Zoran Stijovic is a senior official of the RDB, the State Security Service, or he was at this time. Did you know that Novak was related to a senior official in the State Security Service, or is that something you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I met that man a month ago, perhaps, but I didn't know what he was, and I didn't know -- had no idea that he was related to Novak.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: A month ago from today or a month ago at the time?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From today.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Without turning up the passage in the NGO report that you've been taken to, I just want to read you a passage and see if this is what you had heard; that "on the 24th of March, Serbian police officers killed in flight three Kosovar Albanians, shelled houses in which unarmed civilians had taken cover, placed in jeopardy the lives of children, women, and arrested persons in order to defend themselves, and used the house of the only non-Albanian family as a military facility." Does that fairly describe what you had heard had taken place in Gllogjan just a few weeks before the incident you're describing?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm telling you once again, I'm the wrong person to ask about such things. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You talked to the Stojanovic brothers and to Veselin Stijovic about what happened to them in April, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were you aware that there was a general belief that they had been involved in providing facilities for the police to attack the Haradinaj compound in Gllogjan?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Were you aware that there was a general belief amongst the Albanian population that the Stojanovic house had been used as a facility to launch an attack on Gllogjan? Did you know that was an allegation that was widely believed in the Albanian community?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. You see, you've told us you had some Albanian friends. I want to suggest to you that after Prekaz and Likoshan, after Gllogjan, the Albanian community in that area, ordinary people, were angry and frightened about what might happen again.

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you think.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm asking you what you picked up from the Albanian friends that you knew, Mr. Stijovic. I apologise, Mr. Radosevic.

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what happened in Glodjane and in other villages? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm asking you, from your contacts with Albanian friends that you've told us about, had you not picked up the fact that the villagers in that area were very frightened about the possibility that they were going to be the subject of an attack comparable to what had happened in Prekaz and Likoshan and to what had been attempted in Gllogjan, that they were scared?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, until the very last day when I left Decani, I was on speaking terms, on good terms, with my neighbours. We never spoke about the terrorist army or the police or any such things. I didn't speak about such things with my friends. That's not the kind of thing we discussed. Nor was I interested in what the police and the army or the KLA were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. And nobody had told you, none of your friends had told you, that in the villages around where your parents lived, ordinary people were scared and taking up arms to protect themselves? Nobody told you that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So when you saw these men on the road in Pozhare, that came as a complete surprise to you, did it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The question I asked you -- the question I asked you was whether it came as a complete surprise to see, you've told us, 150 men, most of them in civilian clothing, with weapons out on the streets?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it frightened me and surprised me. I was frightened because I was captured, and I was surprised that something like that could happen at all because I was on good terms with everybody. I had never done any harm to anyone, neither me or my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What was your cousin's job? I'm sorry, you've probably got more than one cousin. Did you have a cousin in the Decani police?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no relatives. I have some friends among the police. Maybe distant relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You're sure that your cousin is not involved in the police or wasn't at the time?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one? Which relative? Which cousin?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just give me a moment. I think you've mentioned his name in your testimony already. Can you remind us of the name of who it was who first contacted you to tell you that your father's body had been found?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to Vule Mircic and Zoran Nikic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Are you related to either of them?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Nikic is a distant relative; nothing close.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Have you described him as a cousin?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said he was a relative but a distant one.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he was the chief of police in Decani, was he?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was komandir, the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was he involved in the 24th of March incident?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I come on to the description that you've given of the men that you saw? You say, first of all, you were stopped in your vehicles by a group of four or five men, two of whom were in uniform, and two or three in civilian clothes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the uniforms didn't match. One was a NATO uniform and one, you said, was a black uniform with red stripes and spots; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. The first one was a NATO uniform, and the other one was red and black, coffee colour, with some dots on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Had you ever seen that uniform anywhere before?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had seen a NATO uniform before. I had not seen the other one, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You said after you were initially stopped, a larger group of other men came out. Can you remind us of the number, approximately?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all hiding in the ditches. There were 50 or 60 of them when they all emerged from where they had been hiding. I was frightened. I didn't really count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Some of them, you said, were in uniform, some of them not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The majority of them in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And some of them, I think, had partial uniforms. In other words, they were wearing civilian clothes perhaps with a pair of fatigue trousers or a camouflage jacket; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with KLA insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you were there at the Pozhare crossroads for, in total, I think, half an hour or thereabouts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think you said yesterday there were 40 of them debating what was going to happen, and who would take you to Gllogjan, and so forth; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I didn't say there were exactly 50 or 60. I said roughly 50, 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But the point I'm making is they were all -- they all had an opinion, is that right, debating amongst themselves, a lot of different opinions being expressed?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And it sounds a pretty chaotic scene you're describing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were discussing between them who would go, who would stay, who would stay with us. It was quite normal for them. They seemed quite happy to have captured us and to be taking us to Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But I'm just putting to you a sentence from the witness statement you made to the Prosecution in January 2002. I don't need you to look at it. But is it right that you couldn't tell who was in charge? I think you said: "I could not ascertain who was actually in charge."

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I couldn't identify the person in charge. I suppose the person in charge was the one who caught me and captured me. But as for determining it on the basis of rank insignia, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But also no one was making clear decisions. It took half an hour to decide what was going to happen to you, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I said it was about half an hour. It could have been 20 minutes; it could have been 45 minutes. Around half an hour they were debating who would go with us, who would accompany us to Glodjane village.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were the men in civilian clothes taking part in this discussion?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I mean, roughly how many people did you see expressing an opinion?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How many? Well, I don't know how many of them expressed an opinion. I know that one of them volunteered to get into the car with us. How many of them expressed an opinion, I really didn't pay attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You've used the word "debating," Mr. Radosevic. More or less than ten involved in this debate?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all talking at the same time. They were arguing whether they would be taking me to Glodjane or not. I thought myself only about one thing and how -- and that was how to get out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, that's very helpful. They were all arguing amongst themselves; nobody clearly in command. You'd agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were arguing amongst them, and who was the main man among them, I really can't tell you. I can't tell you anything if I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to tell me, I'm asking you to describe what you saw. And you've been involved in the police, and so you know how an organisation functions when people have to make decisions if it's properly organised and there's a leadership structure. You know how decisions are taken. But what you're describing for us is a rather different and rather more chaotic picture. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to tell you that I didn't see who the main person was. There were some in uniform, some in civilian clothes, but they were all armed. At that time, I wasn't even trying to establish who the person in charge was. I wasn't interested. The only thing that I was interested in was to get myself, my mother, and my friend out of there. It was not my purpose at the time to establish who the person in charge was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And there was no communication device? You said you didn't see any -- yesterday, when you gave evidence, you didn't see anybody using a communication device, a telephone or a walkie-talkie or anything like that? That's what I think you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I didn't notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So these people weren't receiving instructions from anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then I think on the route towards Gllogjan, you said in your witness statement - again, I don't ask you to turn it up unless we need to - you describe the people you saw along the way as "large numbers of armed men dressed and armed in the haphazard fashion I have described. They were milling around but didn't seem to be moving in any particular direction." Is that a fair description of what you saw?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But you saw them digging trenches, I think you said, at least at one intersection; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, based on your experience, a trench like that is a defensive position, is it not? It's a means of preventing Serb forces or police from entering the area?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were probably doing something for a purpose. Whether it was for the police or something else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, overall, you've described people raising fists and chanting, and I think, if I've added it up correctly, you're talking about having seen in total more than 150 people?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Pozare to Rznic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea of how the number of men you saw would relate to the number of Albanian homes in the areas you're describing? Are we looking at half the male adult Albanian population out on the streets of those villages, or more than half, or less than half?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't answer that question. I don't know how many males lived in Pozare village or in Iluk. I really can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But it must have been a pretty large section, mustn't it, of the Albanian male population of those villages that you say you saw?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a lot of Albanians. I can't say otherwise. I just can't say whether they were all carrying rifles or not. I can tell you only about that day and what I saw from Pozare to Glodjane and from Dasinovac to Decani. I'm talking about that day. Whether they carried arms before that or after that, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But they were all carrying arms on that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group that I saw, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about what happened when the car broke down in a moment or two, but I just want to carry on asking you a little bit more about how these people seemed to you to be behaving, how they seemed to be organised, at various stages in your account. When the car broke down, first of all, I think you described again a situation where people were, amongst themselves, disagreeing about what was going to happen with you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where, in Glodjane village, when we arrived, or in Pozare village?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, in Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived at Glodjane, when the car broke down, when that group that I told you about came, those who had come with us from Pozare returned to Pozare. They didn't talk to us anymore. But they looked happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the place where the car broke down, I mean, that's where all of the incidents that you've described taking place in Gllogjan happened, just where the car had happened to break down; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's some 200 or 300 metres outside of Glodjane. I believe it's still within the area of Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's on the road approaching Gllogjan, 200 to 300 metres outside, on the opposite side of Gllogjan from where your friends, the Stojanovics, lived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. From Rznici to Glodjane looking -- it could have been 500 metres, not necessarily 300. I didn't measure it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Five-hundred metres outside Gllogjan? Sorry, I didn't get an answer to that, Mr. Radosevic. By "500 metres," you mean 500 metres outside of Gllogjan, it could have been?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Rznic to Glodjane, the entrance to Glodjane, that's about 500 metres, if you move from Rznic to Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at the distances on the map, but if that's right, then what you're saying is you were, in fact, stopped nearer to Irzniq than to Gllogjan; is that correct? You've told us 2 to 300 metres, roughly halfway, or, if anything, nearer to Irzniq than Gllogjan? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you the exact number of kilometres, but I'm sure that it's 2 kilometres from Rznic at the very entrance to Glodjane. If that's Glodjane, on the basis of the number of times that I actually travelled down that route, that would be Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But in any event, it's the opposite side, I think you can confirm, of Gllogjan, the opposite road to the road that leads out to the Stojanovics' house?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that road leads from Rznic to the Stojanovics' place. Maybe there is another road, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I'm looking at the clock. Could you find a suitable moment, convenient moment, within the next couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The building that you and Novak Stijovic were taken into, putting it shortly, just happened to be the nearest building to where the car broke down, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And if I can just, before we take a break, complete this topic that I'm asking you some questions about. I want to move to a little later stage in the account that you've given us when you say that you had been to see your father, you had collected a gun, and you had -- you then were stopped by three men, one of whom you knew as Caus. Yes? Do you remember that point in the account?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was Caus in uniform when you met him?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was not wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were the other two men, or either of them, wearing a uniform, the two who were with him when they stopped you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There in the village of Bandera, at the intersection, the three of them were not wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were they armed, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did they stop you, as in pointed their guns at you and required to stop, as it happened in Pozhare?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The two of them pointed their rifles at me, and Caus waved at me to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you've told us that after that, you went with him back to Pozhare, and that whilst you were there, there was again confusion, with half of the people who you'd seen before at the Pozhare crossroads saying you should be allowed to continue and half of them saying you shouldn't; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Caus insisted that I should be allowed to go and fetch the other rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, but you said, of the people at Pozhare, who were the same people who had stopped you earlier, you told us, of that group, half of them wanted to let you carry on and the other half wanted to stop you. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had -- they argued. Some wanted to take me to Glodjane with the rifle that I had surrendered and the others insisted, with Caus at their head, that I should go to Decani to get the other rifle. And Caus, I handed him the rifle, and I don't know what happened with the rifle, whether he kept it for himself or what.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We'll come to that after the break. But the short point I want to put to you is that, in all of these engagements where you were not able to identify anybody in command, the picture that you're painting for us - and it may well be -- I'm not challenging it, I'm just asking you to confirm it - the picture that you're painting for us is of chaotic and disorganised groups of local villagers with weapons in their hands, with no proper system of command or control; some in uniforms and some without. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know how it is. I can't tell you what I didn't see. If I had seen somebody who was in command, who said, Attention, go left, go right, I don't know, maybe there was a commander there, but they were arguing amongst themselves. I can't really tell you now whether there was anyone in charge there or anyone responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be a convenient moment. May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, the Chamber staff received a copy of the information you received from the Mapping Unit. You said the map you used is 1:100.000. The Mapping Unit informed you that the original scale of the map, which was then either reduced or enlarged, was 1:100.000, so it's of no use to tell us what the original map was. That was exactly the point I raised. Therefore, the information you gave is not correct. Just for your information, the actual scale of the map, due to enlarging, is approximately 1:60.000, if that would assist you, and that's fully in accordance with the scale you will find on the satellite photo-map which has been produced in the other binder. You're invited to be more precise in your answers next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can very briefly address you on that, the information should not have gone to the Court in the manner in which it did. What Mr. Dutertre said before is that we will provide the Chamber tomorrow with a map which has a scale written on the side and on the bottom of it. I'm getting the Mapping Unit to provide another map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre said the following: "The map we have been using all the time," and he was referring to P10, P11, and P12, "is 1:100.000, and that is the information that was communicated to me by the investigators through the Map Unit." The message which was sent by the Mapping Unit was that this is a product of pasting cut-outs of original maps, which were 1:100.000, and due to enlarging and reducing, that it's not 1:100.000 anymore. So what's the use of telling us that it is 1:100.000 -- I mean, apart from you provide another map tomorrow. I didn't ask for another map. I just wanted to know what the scale is. I'm not seeking more paper. What I'm seeking is correct information on a question I put to Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will provide the correct information. Would it not assist the Trial Chamber if we were to provide a map in e-court which has the scale down the sides and -- the scale as in 1 kilometre, 2 kilometres, 3 kilometres, so that you can basically see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've done so already by --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's what I want to do. I want to get that before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you did that already by the - could I call it - the Google map, the photograph, satellite photograph. There is a scale on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But it's not the one we're showing. For example, the map Mr. Dutertre showed this witness does not the scale 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 kilometres on the bottom of it. I understand Your Honour's concern. If we get the same map and get the Mapping Unit to put the scale down the sides and on the bottom, everyone will be able to see and do their own calculation as the map is displayed, rather than working out whether it's 1:100.000 or 50.000 or 25, and trying to do that one. We will have the scale underneath in kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Mapping Unit informed you and Mr. Dutertre already that the grid on the map is still 1 kilometre. Whether you enlarge it or whether you reduce it, the grid will be enlarged and reduced to it as well. So there's no need. As a matter of fact, we have already with this information from the Mapping Unit, we have already the information we need, is that -- and I checked that, that one grid, one square on the map, is one square kilometre. Whether you enlarge it, whether you reduce it, that's the scale. So we have it already on it. So there's no need to produce more paperwork, because, as the Mapping Unit has informed you, it's there. But the information was not correct. The information is that due to reducing and resizing, you couldn't make this a map of 1:100.000 anymore, but that the grid still, although it's not anymore 1 centimetre, which it was on the original map, that any square on this map, map number 7, represents 1 square kilometre. So we have everything we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm trying to be of assistance. I'm not privy to the information the Mapping Unit provided apparently during the session. I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was trying to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I'm just saying something about Mr. Dutertre telling us that the map he used was 1:100.000, which it was not. We'll adjourn --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't think he was aware of that when he said it. I think the information came after he said that. An e-mail came to Mr. Smith, our case manager, during the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- let me see whether I can -- I can tell you, at least according to my information, the OTP, Mr. Smith ....

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: According to my information, Mr. Smith was informed of the following: Referring to map 7 and map C in the e-court binder, they were both taken from a montage of the four map sheets listed in the bottom left corner. The original, bold, "Scale of that map was 1:100.000. One centimetre on the map is 1 kilometre on the ground. There is a square-centimetre grid on that map, purple colour, representing a square kilometre in reality. The cut-out areas of this montage in the binder have been reduced or enlarged, as required, for map 6 and map 7, but so far has the square-centimetre grid. Measuring one of those squares is not exactly 1 centimetre anymore, but it still represents a square kilometre in reality." That's the information as it was conveyed to me, which was sent to the OTP, which clearly says the map used is not 1:100.000 anymore due to enlarging. If it's not correct, then please tell me who misinformed me. I read from what I understood to be the message to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not spend any further time on the matter. The matter has been -- but I'm a bit allergic for receiving wrong information, and the wrong information was that the map used was 1:100.000. Whatever was indicated as would follow, that information was wrong. Mr. Dutertre, you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I gave you the information that I read in an e-mail that I received. I was not able to check whether the information was accurate or not. What I did was just give this information to you. I'm extremely sorry if this is -- if there is -- if the information is inconsistent. I'm extremely sorry for the time we have been spending on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would appreciate to receive a copy, if the Defence does not object, to the e-mail you received, because the issue is whether you relayed information you received incorrectly - I blamed you for that, and if I'm wrong I have to correct that - or that you misinterpreted the information and due to such a mistake, you misinformed the Chamber. I would like to know in order to be in a position to apologise if I unjustified -- unjustly blamed you for passing wrong information. So if you would be so kind to provide it to the Chamber during the break, then I will be able to see whether I have to apologise to you. We stand adjourned until ten minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, I didn't receive the information I asked for, but I'm not going to spend any more time on it in court at this very moment. Mr. Emmerson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radosevic, you described the assaults that took place in the roadside outside Gllogjan already. I just want to ask you this: From the description that you've given, it sounds as though Novak Stijovic was assaulted first; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you said it wasn't until you lost control of yourself and physically intervened that anybody tried to assault you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that moment they didn't start to beat me up until he fell down, and then I protected him by turning my back to them, to prevent them from inflicting any more blows to his head and to his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When the first blow was struck to Novak Stijovic, where was he in relation to you? How far away from him were you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a metre, 1 metre. Approximately 1 metre.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because you've told us that nobody hurt your mother and that nobody tried to hurt you until you physically intervened; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I did not physically intervene in the sense of wanting to beat them, to fight with them. I simply couldn't watch them beat my friend. Maybe they wanted to beat me, too, or just him, I don't know. I merely tried to protect him, and then they started beating me. They couldn't beat him anymore because I had put my back to protect him. I turned my back to them so that they couldn't beat him anymore, and then they started beating me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that. Did you see or hear any reason why Novak Stijovic might have been singled out from amongst the three of you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you this: I'm going to read to you a passage from the witness statement that you made in this case on the 26th of January, 2002. I'm not going to ask for it to be brought up unless anybody wants it, but for the record, it's on page 6 and is the fifth full paragraph. You said that whilst you were being questioned and struck, you said this: "They would ask me questions about where my weapon was, who was the police commander in Decani, and who had been shooting at them." I'll read that to you again: "They would ask me questions about where my weapon was, who was the police commander in Decani, and who had been shooting at them." Now, when they were asking you -- first of all, do you remember saying that to the Prosecution investigators?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did say that they had beaten me up. I told them about the numbers. I remember saying that they beat me up in order to make me tell them who had the weapons, who was -- where the police was, and things like that. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The passage I've just put to you I've read from a witness statement that you've signed, Mr. Radosevic, after you told us you'd been interviewed by the Prosecution. This is the statement you've said is the accurate version of events. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, when you were being asked "who had been shooting at them," what did you understand that to be a reference to?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify? What do you mean, who had shot at them?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You told the Prosecution that you were being asked questions, and that one of the questions that you were being asked by the men in the street was "who had been shooting at them." You were being asked to tell them who it was had been shooting at them, and I'm asking you, please, to tell us what was meant? What you understood by that remark or that question?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they probably asked -- were asking about this incident that you referred to when this man --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was killed. I don't know why else. I don't know whether it was really the police or not. They were saying that it was the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So they were saying to you that the police, on the 24th of March, had been shooting at and killing people in Gllogjan. Is that what they were saying?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: From the answer you've just given us, do I understand that they were asking you who had been responsible for shooting and killing civilians in Gllogjan on the 24th of March? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know who was responsible for the 24th of April. Could this be clarified, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you who was responsible; I'm asking you about something you yourself told the Prosecution in a statement that you signed about this case. And you told them that you were being asked by the men who were beating you in the street who it was had been shooting at them, and you have told us that you thought they were referring to the incident on the 24th of March. And I am asking you: Were they asking you about who was responsible for shooting civilians on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They asked me who was in the police. They were asking me such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And they were also asking you, Who was the police commander in Decani, weren't they? Because that's what you told the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you knew who the police commander in Decani was, I suggest, Mr. Radosevic, because it was your cousin Zoran Nikic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He was your cousin, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a distant relative. He's not a close relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Simple -- it's a simple --

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is not a cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He is not a cousin. You're sure about that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a relative, but he's a distant relative. He's not a close relative; he's a distant relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Radosevic, let's be specific. You've just told us he's not a cousin, all right? Can we be clear about that? Are you trying to conceal from this tribunal the nature of your relationship with the Decan police forces?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I've already explained to the Judges that we are related, but he is my distant relative. He is not a cousin. He -- we are distantly related. He is not a close relative of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, we could go on with this for ages.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we not try to find out what the relationship is, so in a more positive way. You say he's not a cousin. I do understand a cousin to be a child of one of your uncles or aunts. Do we agree that we would call such a person a cousin, or am I mixing up nephews and cousins at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that's correct. Is he a child of one of your uncles or aunts; that is, a brother or sister of your father or your mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what he, then, is, if you say -- do you have the same grandfathers? Could you describe to us if you say he is a relative but not a close relative, could you -- if you know, could you tell us what exactly your family relationship is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, this is from the time when they were in Montenegro. So when brothers parted ways, that may have been 200 years ago. Nikics and Radosevics were related at one very distant point in time, but we are not related now. I have all due respect for him, but he is not a close relative. What I consider to be a close relative is somebody who is my uncle or my aunt or their children. That would be the kind of relation that I consider to be close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you said a common ancestor, we should look for such a common ancestor more than a hundred years ago; is that correctly understood? That would be, most likely, great, great, great-grandfather, something like that. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, something like that. They parted ways or the family divided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no common grandfather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not even the great-grandfather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to clarify the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we please look at Defence document identification 148 - is that a 2? - 1484. I'm sorry, I do apologise, 1507. I've given you the wrong reference. It should be 1507.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number D5, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And could we go, please, to the fourth page, page 4 of 7, paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is a passage in a statement where you're describing, Mr. Radosevic, the finding of your father's remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I don't know if we can find the equivalent paragraph in the Serbian translation. We don't have the Serbian translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me read to you -- there is an Albanian translation, but perhaps it's simpler if I read it to you and have it translated. You said: "I was present when the bodies of Slobodan Milosevic and Milos Radunovic were located in by police in September 1998. I was with Zoran Nikic, my cousin." I just need to understand from you, Mr. Radosevic, why it is that in here and in notes of an interview you had with the Prosecution on the 7th of March, you've chosen to refer to Mr. Nikic as your cousin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd very much like to have the original language here, because this Chamber is aware of problems that have arisen on previous occasions on this kind of matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, if there is an Albanian original --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This was, I think, read over to the witness in Serbian before being signed; in other words, it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It complicates it even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we try to go back to the most original language we have, at least the language that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Our belief, and we'll obviously check it, is that this statement was recorded in English and read over to the witness in Serbian, and it's been translated into Albanian for the purposes of the proceedings. So this would be the closest to the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although I do not expect the witness to have given the interview in English; so therefore then we have two or three changes of translation: First to get it on paper and then later to have it --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Read over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- read over and also have it translated. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think if I understood Your Honour correctly, this is a statement where an interview is conducted between an English speaker and this witness through an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that -- unless the witness would speak fluent English --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then recorded in English and read over to the witness by the interpreter in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Most likely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That is our understanding, and then signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Well, proceed as you wish, but at the same time, I would mind you to be aware of possible explanations other than you might elicit -- want to elicit from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radosevic, you were also, I think, interviewed by Mr. Dutertre, who sits on the opposite side of the court, on the 7th of March about your statement via videolink, and we have a record of that interview, and commenting on the paragraph I've just shown you, the record reads: "My cousin Zoran Nikic, chief of police in Decani, was informed that the bodies were located ..." Now, again, I just want to give you an opportunity to be clear. Do you refer, when you are describing Zoran Nikic, do you refer to him as your cousin? Because that's what Mr. Dutertre has recorded.

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we got on well together, but that's a different topic. Zoran Nikic was -- he told me that my father had been found, so the information came from him or from the chief or from the deputy commander. No rank and file police officer could have told me that they had found my father and where they had found him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I'd like to put one question. When you spoke to those who interviewed you and when you described your relationship with Mr. Nikic, do you remember what word you used to express what your family relationship, or your relationship, with Mr. Nikic was? Do you remember the word you used in your own language? Could you just give that word, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They asked me, Who is he to you? I said, Relative, friend; "relative" meaning distant relative. We have a relationship of mutual respect from way back, but I don't understand why counsel is grilling me on this point and splitting hairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the interpreters, perhaps. The word the witness used, is that a word which would make it possible to understand it as a wider relationship rather than a close relationship, such as a cousin? I'm listening to the English channel, so if perhaps the English interpreter could --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Relative" is a very general word and that's the word that the witness used, "rodzak," meaning literally relative. He doesn't specify any kind of relationship close or distant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be -- and I am asking you more or less now as experts, would it be imaginable that if someone uses this word that in a -- well, let's say, a quick translation, it could be interpreted as "cousin"? Is that something you could imagine?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, we should not be answering questions of this kind. There are all sorts of interpretations throughout the former Yugoslavia. Maybe somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I fully respect that you consider yourself not to be in a position to answer this question. Perhaps I should not have asked it. Mr. Emmerson, you may --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this obviously raises, again, the question of -- this was a videolinked proofing session. This raises, again, the question of video-recordings and of the position of Mr. Dutertre in respect of his notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not go over the terrain of Mr. Guy-Smith. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic, Mr. Radosevic. Can I ask you this: You told these men that neither you nor Novak had a gun but that your fathers had hunting rifles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was that the truth, that neither of you had a gun?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, that I didn't have a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And Novak?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because when you went back after you'd visited your father and were stopped at the crossroads in Pozhare for a second time, you told us that you told them that you were going to collect Novak's semi-automatic. Now, first of all, was it a semi-automatic, as you understood it, that you were going to collect?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to find a pretext, and I used the pretext of going to get the automatic rifle to get out of there. I had a hunting rifle, in actual fact, but I had to tell lies to get out of that situation. So what I said was I was going to get that hunting rifle -- I mean, if I said I had intended to go and get a hunting rifle, maybe he wouldn't have let me go.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you -- the truth was you were going to get Novak's father's hunting rifle, but you told them it was a semi-automatic; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned I took that carbine. My father told me, If you can, you run to Decani; you don't go back to Glodjane. So I told those people in Pozare, I told Caus, I'm going to get another rifle. One man said, No, you can't go; another one asked me, Which rifle are you going to get? I said, An automatic rifle. So I was trying everything to get out of there. I could have easily said I was going to get a cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that. So the position is you were lying to the men at the crossroads, I understand that, and I understand the reasons that you've given for it. Were you going to Decan to get Novak's father's hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Decani. When they let me go, I went to the police station to report what had happened to me, and from there they took me to the health centre to be bandaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Where did Novak's father live?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Bandera, near Ljubarda. I don't know whether it's officially Bandera or Ljubarda. I think that officially it's Bandera.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So there was no gun or weapon belonging to that family in Decan?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which family?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The Stijovic family, either father or son. There was no gun in Decan?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dropped by that house, but there was nobody there. Whether the rifle was at Bandera or in Decani, I really don't know. Three-hundred metres on, I was stopped by Caus ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you dropped by the Bandera house, did you, in -- the Stijovics' house in Bandera, did you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Have you told -- have you ever told anybody that before, Mr. Radosevic?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And there was nobody there?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What was your intention in going there?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to find somebody to get hold of another rifle that would enable me to get my mother and Novak out.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you were going to the house to get Novak's father's rifle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was on my way to my house, on my way to Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, let's just be clear. When did you go to Bandera? Was it before or after you'd been to your father?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got the rifle from my father, I continued to Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you got the rifle from your father, you went to the Pozhare crossroads with Caus, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not Pozare, it's Bandera, some 300 metres away. It was the name of the village, Bandera. From there, Caus and I got into a car, took that rifle from my house and went to Pozare.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So it was at the time that you were stopped by Caus that you went to the house of the Stijovics, was it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Before Caus stopped me, before that, I stopped at the Stijovic house. There was nobody there. And from there I went to Pozare, and then Caus stopped me at the intersection leading to Gornji and Donji Ratis and to Ljubarda on another side.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. I have a little more for this witness, and I think, unless I misread the Court, it's probably the appropriate moment to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. Emmerson, just for my understanding. I have, of course, carefully looked at the map and to the routes the witness has marked as the routes he took. I -- from my recollection, he said how he went from Glodjane to Dasinovac. That's where, from what I understand, his father was. And then the witness indicated how he went from Dasinovac to Decani. And on the map I see, but please correct me when I'm wrong, that the last -- whether it's a village or not is another matter, but the last name before Pozare is Bandera, which is right on the route from -- because he took the southerly road and not the northerly road from Dasinovac to Pozare. Is that a correct understanding of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I need to check the markings because I haven't got a copy of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you have them as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I remember that he took the southerly -- the black road rather than the yellow road and then off.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what's clear on my map.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Bandera is on route between Dashinoc and Pozhare via the southern road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The point I was asking the witness about was the fact that he's never, as far as we're aware at least, mentioned this event at any point in any of his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you went a bit farther than asking him whether he mentioned it ever. You also said from Pozare, did you then go to where it is -- seems to be the road --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That having been clarified, before we adjourn, I've got one tiny little question. I understand that the communication between Mapping Unit, OTP, Registry, and Chambers concerning the map information have caused some concern or may even have upset a bit. The Defence -- if we would pay further attention to it, the Defence is invited to attend whatever communication there will be on the matter, but if it's limited to that, are you interested to attend, or do you say, because the Chamber usually does not engage in any conversations with parties or at least without full transparency, is this a matter you'd like to be fully informed of? We're limited to communications and who took what step at what time and not any substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: For my part, I am entirely content to leave it in Your Honours' hands. If there is information which emerges which may in any way be relevant to the Defence -- -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't expect that, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- then I'm content for Your Honour to exercise that judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm in the exact same position, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Wouldn't surprise Your Honours to hear that I'm in the same position, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00, same courtroom -- Before I finally do, Mr. Guy-Smith, it seems that you -- if there's anything you'd like to raise, if you can wait until tomorrow morning, we'd prefer that, because of course another Chamber is -- if not, you're at least encouraged next time to say it a bit in advance before we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I raised it at the beginning of today's proceedings and it was suggested it be dealt with at the break. I'll raise it tomorrow. It deals with UNMIK issues, once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed about that, and we decided that we will ask for an update tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So, therefore, I said to courtroom II tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
